caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No. 106 of 1980
lawyer:
Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed with Mr. SM Nurul Alam, Advocates ----- For the Appellant.
Mr. Nazmul Huda with Mrs. Sigma Huda Mr. SM Mahbub Elahi and Mr. Mizanur Rahman Bhuiyan, Advocates ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Sheikh Salimuddin ----- Appellant
Vs.
Ataur Rahman and ors ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
2. The plaintiffs case, in brief, is that defendant No. 1 being owner of the suit lands proposed through defendant No. 2 to sell out the suit-lands to the plaintiff and the price was settled at Tk. 25,000/- by mutual agreement in presence of witnesses and some of the defendant Nos. 2-11. The plaintiff paid Tk. 10,000/- as earnest money to defendant No. 1 on 7.12.69 in presence of the witnesses and the defendant No. 1 executed a bainapatra in the same sitting. It was stipulated that he would execute and register a kabala within three years thereof on receipt of the balance money. Defendant No.1 also delivered possession of the suit-lands in favour of the plaintiff as part performance of the contract. The defendant No.1 received a further sum of Tk. 8.000/- from the plaintiff on 24.2.71 and acknowledged the same by putting LTI on a receipt as his right hand was badly affected in catching fish. The plaintiff along with his family members has been residing in the huts of the homestead in the' suit land since the day of bainapatra. In the month of May, 1971 the plaintiff requested the defendant No. 1 himself and through some other defendants to execute and register the kabala on receipt of the balance consideration money but the defendant No.1 did not show any interest to do so. Thereafter the plaintiff approached his relation Al-haj Mohammad Ali, Advocate, to take legal steps in the matter and made over the bainapatra and the receipt to him for the purpose. Then the country was seriously involved in the war of liberation and his huts excepting two were razed and burnt away by Pakistan Army. After the war of liberation the plaintiff met Mr. Mohammad Ali, Advocate, to know what steps were taken by that time. The learned Advocate then told the plaintiff that he (plaintiff) had received back the bainapatra and the receipt. The plaintiff thereafter tried to find out the aforesaid papers but could not. The facts of non-availability of the bainapatra was known to all including the defendants and taking advantage of this situation the defendant No.1 brought a false suit being MS No. 84 of 1972 in the 1st Court of Munsif, Dhaka claiming Tk. 2.000/- from the present plaintiff as compensation for barga crops for two years. The plaintiff appeared, in that suit and 16.5.73 was fixed for filing written statement. Thereafter there was talk for compromise and in that suit defendant No. 1 admitted to have agreed to sell the suit property to the present plaintiff and he also aumntca delivery of possession of the suit property in favour of the present plaintiff as part performance of the contract. But due to paucity of time the said compromise could not be effected and it was decided that another sitting would be held for the purpose. Accordingly, the present plaintiff requested his Advocate's clerk to take time in that suit. But the clerk took a wrong date and subsequently on scrutiny it was found that the suit was already decreed ex parte on 30.5.73. The plaintiff then filed a Misc. Case under Order 9 rule 13 CPC and the same Wells also dis- missed for default on 11.3.74. The present plaintiff, of course, at a later date instituted a suit for setting aside the said ex parte decree which was still pending. Meanwhile the present plaintiff came to know that the defendant No. 1 transferred the suit lands to the defendant Nos. 2-11 and others without any consideration by registered deeds. It is alleged that the said Mr. Mohammad Ali ultimately found out the bainapatra and the receipt from his father-in-law's house at Narayangonj where he shifted during the war of liberation and that despite requests, the defendant No. 1 has not come forward to register the sale deed in favour of the plaintiff. Hence the present suit. 

 3. Defendant Nos. 2, 9 and 10 filed a written statement challenging the facts of the plaint but did not appear before the Court to contest the suit. The defendant No. 1 the appellant filed a separate written statement to contest the suit. His case, inter alia, is that there is no cause of action; that the suit is not maintainable in its present form and the same is barred by limitation. His further case is that he is the owner of the suit land and he did never enter into any contract with the plaintiff to sell out the same nor receive any bainanama from the plaintiff. It is also alleged that the plaintiff did not cultivate the suit land as bargadar under this defendant; that the alleged bainanama and the receipt are all false and fabricated documents. This defendant never received the earnest money of Tk. 10,000/- or the additional payment of Tk.8,000/- as alleged. The plaintiff and his father were bargadars under this defendant. They paid the share of crops to this defendant for some time but then they started defaulting in paying the same. Hence a Money Suit No. 84 of 1972 was instituted against him and the same was decreed and the decree was put into execution and there was an order of attachment of the property of the present plaintiff judgment-debtor. But upon execution of a surety bond by him, his property was saved from attachment. It is further stated that this defendant ultimately sold away his entire property to other defendants who are in possession of the same. The plaintiff never proposed to this defendant to purchase the suit land and as such the suit is fraudulent, speculative and liable to be dismissed with Costs. 

 3. Had the plaintiff capacity to enter into the contract? 

 4. Is the plaintiff entitled to get the decree as prayed for? 

 5. What relief, if any, the plaintiff is entitled to ? 

 5. The plaintiff examined in all 6 PWs and the defendant No. 1 examined 4 DWs in support of their respective cases and both the sides filed some documents. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the materials on record decreed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 24.7.80 holding, inter alia. that the LTI in Ext. 5 is not the LTI of defendant No. 1 and the statement of the plaintiff for further payment of Tk.8,000/- on 24.2.71 to the defendant No. 1 as an advance payment of the consideration money cannot be accepted but the deed of agreement Ext.4 was duly executed by the defendant No. 1 and on the date of execution he received an advance consideration of Tk. 10,000/- from the plaintiff. So the deed of agreement is genuine and valid. 

 9. His first submission is that Ute plaintiff has totally failed to prove by reliable and sufficient evidence the alleged contract for sale and the execution of the bainapatra Ext. 4 by the defendant appellant in favour of the plaintiff-respondent and as such the impugned judgment and decree are liable to be set aside. In this connection his further submission is that the witnesses for the plaintiff arc all close relations and they arc highly interested. Besides, their evidences are discrepant on material particulars, but the learned Subordinate Judge without weighing the evidence in its true and correct perspective, arbitrarily and illegally held that the alleged contract in between the plaintiff and the defendant No.1 and the execution of the bainapatra Ext. 4 in pursuance thereof are genuine and most illegally decreed the suit. 

 11. His last submission is that under section 22 of the Specific Relief Act the decree for specific performance of a contract is a discretionary one of ; the Court and in the present case even if the contract is proved to be valid still then in view of the subsequent transfer of the suit lands to defendant Nos. 2-11 and their claim of possession over the same, the decree if passed in favour of the plaintiff will put the defendants into serious hardships and give the plaintiff an unfair advantage over the defendants and, as such, the present decree in favour of the plaintiff should be refused subject to payment of reasonable solatium to him by the defendants-appellant. 

 12. Mr. Nazmul Huda, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-respondent, on the other hand, submits that the submissions made on behalf of the defendant are not correct and tenable in law and on facts. He submits that the witnesses though related to the Plaintiffs are quite dependable and trustworthy and they have satisfactorily proved the bainapatra in question and the execution of the bainapatra Ext. 4 and as such learned Subordinate Judge has rightly passed the impugned judgment and decree in favour of the plaintiff-respondent. His further submission is that it is true that no specific issue has been framed on the question of possession, but in fact that question has been sufficiently discussed by the Trial Court, and as such there was no illegality in not framing a specific issue on possession. As to the last submission of the learned Advocate that the relief under the Specific Relief Act is discretionary and that in the instant case if the suit is decreed, the plaintiff will have unfair advantage over the defendant and as such the prayer for decree should be refused on condition of payment of solatium to the plaintiff, the learned Advocate for the respondent submits that it is not disputed that the relief for specific performance of a contract is a discretionary one but in the instant case when the defendant No. 1 had already divested himself of the entire property by executing the registered sale deeds in favour of defendant Nos. 2-11, there is no scope of getting any unfair advantage by the plaintiff over the contesting defendant No. 1 

 13. Now, let us consider the above submissions of the learned Advocates in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record. From the impugned judgment it appears that the learned Subordinate Judge took up all the issues except issue No. 5 for consideration and decided them in favour of the plaintiff and in answer to issue No. 5, he opined that the plaintiff was entitled to get relief in the suit and accordingly decreed the same. 

 14. Let us take up the first point raised by the learned Advocate for the appellant as to whether the alleged contract and the execution of the bainanama Ext. 4 have been sufficiently proved by the plaintiff, by cogent and reliable evidence. The plaintiff, as has been stated above, examined in all 6 witnesses including himself as PW 3 in support of his case and the defendant No. 1, the present appellant, adduced evidence of 4 DWs including himself as DW 1 to establish his case. 

 15. PW. 1 Fazle Murshed Khan is finger print expert attached to CID Bangladesh. He received the alleged bainapatra Ext. 4 dated 7.12.69 containing the alleged finger impression of Defendant No. 1 Shaikh Salimuddin marked as C, C1 and C2 and also one receipt Ext. 5 dated 24.2.71 showing additional alleged advance payment of the consideration money amounting to Tk. 8,000/- by the plaintiff containing finger print therein as C3. He obtained specimen finger impressions of defendant No. 1 on some blank papers on 17.11.78 for comparison and opinion and the same was marked as B. He got the impression enlarged by photograph compared the same and then opined that the finger impression marked CI and C2 i.e. the impression on the second page of the alleged bainapatra Ext. 4 are identical with the specimen L TI marked B but the finger impressions marked as C and C3 that the impression on the first page of the Ext. 4 are not identical with the finger impression marked B. He gave his report Ext. 1. In his cross-examination he stated that all the LTIs. did not appear to have been super-imposed. PW 2 Md. Abdul Halim is a hand-writing expert. He received the alleged unregistered bainapatra Ext. 4 dated 7.12.69 in two sheets containing signatures in Bengali reading Sk. Salim uddin marked as 'A, AI and A2 and one written statement dated 23.4.76 in connection with TS No. 502 of 1974 marked as B to B4 and the specimen signatures of defendant No. 1 Sk. Salimuddin in Bengali in four sheets marked as C to C3. He obtained necessary photographic enlargement of the same and after comparison gave his opinion as follows: One signature marked AI and A2 i.e. the signature of Sk. Salimuddin of the second page of Ext. 4. The alleged bainapatra agreed with the specimen signature marked as C series in various respects as stated in the report and the signatures marked A1 and A2 and C series are the products of one and the same hand but the signatures marked B series differ from the signatures marked as C series and A series both in general and individual characteristic of writings fundamentally. His further opinion is that the signatures marked B series have not been executed by the author who executed the signature marked C and A series. He expressed no definite opinion as to the signature marked A with his signature on the first page of Ext. 4 as the same had got both agreement and disagreement of the signatures marked as A1, A2 and C series. He proved his report Ext. 2 and the enlarged photograph Ext. C series. 

 16. PW 3 Ataur Rahman the plaintiff who is a Jamai of Haizuddin and Bhagni Jamai of PW 5. Habibur Rahman stated, inter alia, in his deposition that defendant No.1 as owner of the suit land measuring 8.50 acres proposed to sell the same to him for a consideration of Tk. 25,000/- in presence of defendant Nos. 2-11 and on 7.12.69 sitting in the house of PW 5 Habibur Rahman at 10 AM he executed a bainapatra to that effect on receipt of Tk. 10,000/- as earnest money in presence of Haizuddin, Habibur Rahman, Anwarul Huq, Abdul Mannan and Mosleuddin, This witness stated that Abdur Rashid PW 4 was the scribe of the bainapatra. He proved the bainapatra Ext. 4. He stated that he got possession of the suit land from the defendant No. 1 at about 3 to 3.30 PM. He further stated that defendant No. 1 again received a sum of Tk. 8,000/- as advance payment from him after granting receipt thereof Ext. 5 dated 24.2.71 written by Kazi Abdur Rashid PW 4. He stated that defendant No. 1 could not sign the receipt as he was unable to do so due to a sting from a fish. He stated that Anwarul Huq, Habibur Rahman (PW 5) and Haizuddin who were present at the time of receipt of the said amount signed the said receipt. He proved the receipt Ext 5. He sated that he erected a kitchen and cow-shed in the suit property and has been possessing the same. He further stated that it was stipulated that the deed of sale would be executed and registered within 3 years from the date of bainapatra. He stated that in May, 1971 he tendered the balance money and requested defendant No. 1 in presence of the other defendants tCl execute and register the kabala deed but the defendant No. 1 refused Cl do so. Then the plaintiff handed over the Bainapatra and the receipt Exts. 4 and 5 respectively to his Mamashasur Advocate Md. Ali to take legal steps in the matter who shifted to his father-in-law's house at Narayangonj for safety during the war of liberation of Bangladesh. He further stated that his file was misplaced and not traceable for some time, but the same was ultimately recovered from the possession of the said Mr. Mohammad Ali and thereafter the present suit was filed: He stated that the defendant Nos. 2-11 were aware of the bainapatra. He further. stated that the defendant No. 1 started a false suit being Money Suit No. 84 of 1972 in the 1st Court of Munsif, Dhaka against him for barga crops for two years and got an ex parte decree. He filled a Misc. Case under Order 9, rule 11 CPC against the said ex parte decree but same was dismissed for default and then he filed a regular suit being TS No. 607 of 1974 for setting aside the ex parte decree and that was pending. In cross-examination, he stated that on 2.12.69 the talk of sale first started. He stated that he purchased the stamp at Kathal Bagan and Haizuddin, Habibur Rahman, Anwarul Huq, Mosleuddin, Abdur Rahman and defendant No. 1 were present at the time of writing the bainapatra and it was 10 AM. when the same was written and executed. He stated that he got married in June, 1971 and that he did not make any tagada to defendant No. 1 before May, 1971. He stated that probably it was in 1973 for the first time, he came to know that the documents were not traceable from his Advocate. He denied the suggestion that at the instance of Haizuddin and Habibur Rahman he purchased the stamp papers of the bainapatra Ext. 4 much later than its date of execution for illegally grabbing the suit land and further to hide the date of purchase of the stamp he purposely pasted papers on the back of the stamp papers. He stated that defendant No. 1 was the owner of the lands by a deed of power of attorney. He denied the suggestion that defendant No. 1 did not execute Ext. 4 and he had no capacity to purchase the suit land. He denied that he and his father barga cultivated the suit land under defendant No.1. 

 17. PW 4 Kazi Abdur Rashid is the deed writer. He stated that he wrote the bainapatra which was read over to defendant No. 1 who received Tk. 10,000/- from the plaintiff and signed and also put the LTI on Ext. 4. He further stated that the plaintiff further paid Tk. 8,000/- to defendant No. 1 in his presence and in presence of other witnesses. He stated to have written Ext. 5. the receipt of Tk. 8,000/-, In cross-examination he stated that he passed the Ma- tribulation Examination in 1969 and started writing deeds from May/June, 1969 and he had no licence at the time of writing the Ext. 4. He admitted his relationship with the plaintiff. He stated that Haizuddin, Habibur Rahman, Anwarul Huq, defendant No. 1, the plaintiff and 2/3 others whom he did not know were present at the time of writing and execution of Ext 4. He stated that he wrote Ext. 4 sitting in the house of Habibur Rahman PW 5. He denied the suggestion that Ext. 4 was not written on the date as mentioned in it and that it was subsequently written. He denied that Ext. 5 was manufactured. He stated that he had written the deed sitting in the house of Habibur Rahman in the afternoon. He denied the suggestion that he was deposing falsely as the plaintiff was his relation. 

 18. PW 5 Habibur Rahman stated that the plaintiff was his Bhagni Jamai. He stated that the bainapatra was made between defendant No. 1 and the plaintiff and the price was fixed at Tk. 25,000/- and Abdur Rashid was his scribe and that the plaintiff paid Tk. 10,000/- to defendant No.1 on the date of execution of the bainapatra and defendant No. 1 signed the same and put his LTI therein. He also stated that the plaintiff further paid Tk. 10,000/- to defendant No. 1 subsequently and one Abdur Rashid wrote the receipt of the said payment and the defendant No. 1 put his LTI thereon. He proved Ext. 5. He stated that he was the attesting witness in Exts. 4 and 5 and that Mr. Mohammad Ali was his brother. In cross-examination, he stated that he was not present at the time of the talk of sale. He came to know about the sale about Ii hours before the writing of Ext 4. He further stated that the plaintiff, Kazi Abdur Rashid, Haizuddin, defendant No. 1, himself and 2 others were present at the time of writing Ext 4. He stated that Haizuddin was his bhagnipati and deed writer Abdur Rashid was his brother-in-law who used to live with him. He stated that Haiiuddin came to his house at about 9 AM and Ext. 5 was written at about 3 PM. in his house in presence of Abdur Rashid, Haizuddin, himself, the plaintiff and the defendant No 1. He denied the suggestion that he was deposing falsely at the instance of the plaintiff and that no such bainapatra was executed and that Ext. 4 was subsequently written. 

 19. PW 6 Abdul Latif Mia is another relation of the plaintiff. He stated that 10/11 years before, there was a talk of sale of the suit land by the defendant No. 1 to the plaintiff. He, Abdul Hai, Abdus Sattar, Dut Mia, Hossain and others were present in that talk. In cross-examination he stated that the plaintiff was his cousin sister's husband. He could not remember the date of the talk of sale and frankly admitted that he was not present at the time of passing of the earnest money and also was not present at the time of execution of the deed of agreement Ext 4. He denied the suggestion that he was deposing falsely as the plaintiff was his bhagnipati. He denied the suggestion that there was no talk of such sale. 

 20. Now, let us see the evidence led on behalf of the defendant No. 1. DW 1 Sk. Salimuddin is the defendant No. 1 himself, He stated that there was no talk of sale of the suit land in between himself and the plaintiff, He denied the LTI and also the signature in Ext. 4 as his own. He also denied to have received the earnest money of Tk. 10,000/-and further a sum of Tk. 8,000/- from tile plaintiff. He denied his LTI in Ext. 5 the alleged receipt of Tk. 8,000/- as his own. He denied the fact that the defendants 2- 11 were present at the time of the alleged talk of sale of the suit land. He stated that he gave barga of 2/3 kanies of the suit land to the plaintiff on condition that he (plaintiff) would give defendant No.1 half of the the crops but after some time he refused to deliver the same and hence the Money Suit No. 84 of 1972 was filed by this defendant and the same was decreed against him (the present plaintiff) and subsequently the said decree was put into execution and accordingly an order of attachment was issued against the judgment-debtor i.e. the present plaintiff. The plaintiff, of course. filed a suit bearing TS. No. 607 of 1974 against the said ex parte decree which was still pending. He stated that the Government transferred the entire suit land to him executing and registering a deed Ext. D in his favour in 1970. He admitted to have sold the entire property to the present defendants 2-11. He denied the plaintiffs claim of possession over the suit land. He also denied payment of Tk. 10,000/- and 8,000/- by the plaintiff to him. He asserted that the plaintiff did never pay him any money as he had no capacity to pay. The father of the plaintiff was a day laborer and he himself was serving in a bamboo shop. He denied the execution of the receipt Ext 5. He also denied the alleged talk of sale of the suit lands. He asserted that the plaintiff was his bargader for one acre of land. He denied to have given the delivery of possession of the suit land to the plaintiff in pursuance of the alleged bainapatra Ext. 4. He also denied the suggestion that the subsequent purchaser did not give him any consideration money or that they were not in possession of the suit land. He stated that the claim of the plaintiff was false and fraudulent. 

 21. DW 2 Abdul Hye is defendant No. 3 in the suit. He stated that he was not present at the alleged talk of sale of the suit land between the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1. He also denied that the alleged talk of sale was made through him. He asserted that other defendants were also not present at the time of the alleged talk of sale. He stated that he purchased 0.47 acres of the suit land in 1974 from defendant No. 1 and subsequently sold the same to one Idris Ali and Yunus Ali who were in possession of the same. He proved the deed of sale Ext. B. He also denied the fact of any salish regarding the sale or purchase of the suit land between the plaintiff and defendant No.1. He denied the plaintiffs possession in the land. He asserted that he purchased the suitland of Salim, defendant No. 1, as a bonafide purehaser without having any knowledge of the alleged agreement between the plaintiff and the defendant No.1. The purchasers are in possession of the suit land. He denied that Dud Mia, Abdus Satter, Hossain Mohammad and others were present at the talk of sale. He stated that he and Samiruddin were Jimma of the plaintiff for the decretal amount. He denied the suggestion that he purchased a portion of the suit-land without consideration and with knowledge of the bainapatra of the plaintiff. He also denied the suggestion that the plaintiff possessed the entire suit land. Rather he asserted that the plaintiff did never possess the suit land. 

 22. DW 3 Rupsona is another bargadar of defendant No. 1. He stated that he barga cultivated 5/6 kanis of the suit land under defendant No. 1 for five years. He stated that the plaintiff barga cultivated the suit land after him, but could not say how many pakhis of land the plaintiff had barga cultivated. 

 24. He stated that the plaintiff did not possess the suit land, then said that the plaintiff barga cultivated the suit land for two years. He also denied that any salish had taken place in the village regarding the alleged contract for sale of the suit land. In his cross- examination, he denied to have given any threat to dispossess the plaintiff from the suit land. He stated that the plaintiff barga cultivated 2 or 2-1/2 pakhis of the suit land under defendant No. 1. He denied the suggestion that the plaintiff was possessing the suit land by virtus of bainanama Ext. 4. He also denied the suggestion that the plaintiff had business and that he paid the baina money by selling his mother's property. 

 25. Admittedly the plaintiff and the PWs. except the official witnesses namely, PW 1 and PW 2, are close relations. PW 3 is the plaintiff. PW 4 is the brother-in-law of PW 5 and lives with him. PW 5 is mamashasur of the plaintiff. PW 6 is the brother-in-law of the plaintiff. Apart from that one Haizuddin, alleged to have been present at the time of execution of Ext’s. 4 and 5 in the house of the father-in-law of the plaintiff, has not been examined by the plaintiff. Now, about the alleged talk of sale of the suit land. PW 3 the plaintiff stated that the said talk took place on 2.12.69 in presence of the defendants but one of the defendants i.e. No. 3 has deposed in this suit as DW 2. He categorically denied his presence in any alleged talk of sale of the suit property. There is no witness to corroborate PW 3 the plaintiff about the alleged talk of sale except PW 6 who is also a relation and seems to be highly interested. He could not give the date of the alleged talk of sale. DW 1 as well as DW 2 and DW 4 rightly denied holding of any such talk of sale of the suit land between the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1 Thus, it appears that there is no cogent and reliable evidence to establish the factum of the alleged talk of sale. 

 26. Let us now see whether the plaintiff has been able to prove the contract and the execution of the bainapatra Ext. 4. In this regard the plaintiff has produced the evidence of PWs 1-5 to prove the alleged contract of the execution of bainapatra Ext. 4. PW 1 is the finger print expert. He has given his report Ext. 1 which shows that the finger impression marked C1 and C2 in Ext. 4 the bainapatra agreed with the specimen impression of the defendant No.1 in separate papers marked Ext. B but the finger impression marked C3 does not tally with the finger impression of Sk. Salim uddin defendant No. 1 in Ext. B. That means the finger impression marked C3 on the front page of Ext. 4 is not identical with these marked as CI and C2 in the second page of the same. Similarly the signature of Sk. Salim uddin marked Ext. A1 and A2 and his admitted specimen signature marked C are found to be the product of one and the same hand, but signature marked A in the front page of Ext. 4 does not seem to be so. It is well settled that evidence of an expert witness is of very weak nature. The evidence and the opinion of the expert deserve consideration like any other evidence but such evidence has to be received with great caution. It has been held in many cases that of all kinds of evidence, the evidence of an expert is of very weak character. In the case of Eklas Khan and ors. Vs. Prajesh Chandra Das alld ors. reported in BLD 1987 (AD) 142, it has been held that an expert's opinion, particularly of a hand writing expert, is always received with great caution. So in assessing or evaluating the evidence particularly the evidence of hand writing experts on the question of genuineness of a signature, the following facts must be kept in view: (1) very few people sign in the same manner on all occasions, (2) Expert opinion on the genuineness of the signature should be received with great caution especially in a case when there is positive evidence of persons who saw a person sign. 3) All the test evidence by the expert in the matter of comparison of hand writing and signature are merely tentative in character. 4) Opinion is a weak evidence. 

 27. So, keeping the above factors in view, we have-to assess the evidence of PW s 1 and 2. Now, PW 3 is the plaintiff himself. He says that 7 persons were present at the time of writing of the bainapatra and payment of earnest money of Tk. 10,000/- namely, Haizuddin, Habibur Rahman, Anwarul Huq, Abdul Mannan, and his scribe Abdur Rashid PW 4. In cross-examination,  he stated that he purchased stamp papers at lathal Bagan and Habibur Rahman, Anwarul Huq, Abdur Rashid and defendant No.1 were only present when the bainapatra was executed. But PW 4, the alleged scribe, said that Anwarul Hoque, Haizuddin, Habibur Rahman and 2/3 others were present at the time of writing and executing Ext. 4 the bainanama. He admits that he is a relation of pW 3, the plaintiff. PW 5 Habibur Rahman is admittedly a mamashasur of the plaintiff. He stated about execution of Exts. 4 and 5 and payment of the earnest money of Tk. 10,000/- and further payment of Tk. 8,000/- by the plaintiff to defendant No. 1. He stated that he himself along with the plaintiff PW 3, the scribe PW 4 and the defendant No.1 and two others were present at the time of writing the Exhibit 4. He admitted that Haizuddin was his bhagnipati and the deed writer Abdur Rashid was his brother-in-law who used to live with him. He SUited that Ext. 5 the receipt was written at 3 PM on that date in his house in presence of Abdur Rashid, Haizuddin, himself and the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1. Now it appears from the evidence of the aforesaid PWs that there was a good number of persons allegedly present at the time of execution of the bainapatra Ext. 4 and the receipt. Ext. 5, but out of them only the close relations of the plaintiff. PW 3, namely, PW 4 and PW 5 have been examined. The material witnesses alleged to have been present at the time of execution of Exts, 4 and 5, namely, Anwarul Huq, Abdul Mannan, Moslemuddin, Haizuddin had not been produced to support the case of the plaintiff. 

 28. Along with this, let us consider another aspect of the case of the plaintiff, It is an admitted fact that pasting of additional papers on the back of both the pages of Ext. 4 the bainanama, has been done in such a manner that the vendor's name, number and date of purchase of the stamps, etc. have been totally blocked and covered. From the evidence on record, it does not appear that the plaintiff has explained by any evidence as to why and under what circumstances such pasting was required to be done. Besides, to prove the genuineness of the purchase or the stamps on the alleged date of execution of Ext. 4, the plaintiff could have produced the vendor with his register in the Court, but no attempt has been made to do so. Apart from that, another circumstance has to be taken into consideration. It is the case of the plaintiff that he met defendant No. 1 in the month of May, 1971 and requested him to execute the deed in his favour on receipt of the balance money, but defendant No.1 refused to do so. Thereafter he handed over these papers, Exts. 4 and 5 to one Mr. Mohammad Ali; Advocate to take necessary steps and meanwhile there was war of liberation and after the war of liberation he asked Mr. Mohammad Ali as to what steps were taken with regard to the said exhibits but Mr. Mohammad Ali could not produce the same and rather he told the plaintiff that he (plaintiff) had already taken back the said exhibits. Then after some time these Exts. 4 and 5 were recovered from the possession of the said learned Advocate from the house of his father-in-law at Narayangonj and thereafter this suit was instituted on the basis of these exhibits. But this version of the plaintiff has not been substantiated by any evidence nor the said learned Advocate, Mr. Mohammad Ali has been produced to prove the same in this case by the plaintiff to establish the alleged fact of missing of Exts. 4 and 5. Defendants case is out and out a denial of the contract and the execution of the said documents Exts.4 and 5. of the 4 DWs, DW 1, the defendant No. 1 has totally denied the alleged contract for sale of the suit land as well as the execution of the bainanama Ext. 4 and the receipt Ext. 5. DW 2 who is defendant No. 3 in this suit also denied, his presence as well as the presence of other defendants at the alleged talk of sale. DW 4 was a Chairman of Satarkul Union Council. He also denied such talk of sale or the contract for sale of the suit land and the alleged possession of the plaintiff in part performance of such contract between the defendant No. 1 and the plaintiff. We have ourselves scrutinised the Exts, 4 and 5 and compared the finger impressions as well as the signatures as appeared in both the pages of the bainapatra Ext. 4 along with the admitted specimen finger impressions and signatures of defendant No.1, Sk. Salim uddin and we find that the finger impressions and the signatures appearing on the first page of Ext. 4 do not tally with those of the second page of Ext. 4 and it is very difficult to hold that those are the products of the same and one hand. The learned Subordinate Judge, it appears from the judgment has considered the most important issue No.2 as regardsthe genuineness of the deed of agreement and the passing of consideration money thereon in a wrong perspective and through a slipshod manner. He has without discussing the evidence on record, arbitrarily come to a finding that in his opinion, the signatures and the LTIs of the defendant No.1 in Ext. 4, the Bainapatra on the 1st page and the signatures and the LTI on page 2 in Ext. 4 are the products of the one and the same hand and held that Ext. 4 was duly executed by defendant No.1. Of course, with regard to the receipt Ext. 5, it appears in the facts and circumstances of the case that the LTI appearing in Ext. 5 is not the LTI of defendant No. 1. So, the further payment of Tk. 8,000/- as alleged by the plaintiff vide Ext. 5 Was not believed and accepted by the Trial Court rightly. It appears that the learned Subordinate Judge has also misread the evidence. In the judgment he has observed that PWs 3-6 have also stated that the plaintiff has been, possessing the suit land not as a bargader but in part performance of the aforesaid contract, but on perusal of the evidence, it is found that the above observation is not correct. Apart from that, he has accepted the evidence of the said PWs. without examining their trustworthiness, when admittedly they are closely related with each other. It may be pointed out that some material witnesses as stated above have not been produced by the plaintiff in support of his case without any explanation. Thus, when all the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record are considered in their true perspective, only inference that can be drawn is that Ext. 4 the bainanama and Ext. 5 the receipt of further payment are not at all genuine but forged and manufactured documents created by the plaintiff with ulterior motive. Of course, with regard to Ext. 5 the Trial Court has already found that the same is a forged and fabricated document and additional payment of Talc. 8,000/00 by the plaintiff to the defendant has not been proved and against this finding of the Trial Court. the plaintiff has not filed any cross-objection and as such the said finding is still holding good. 

 29. It has been submitted on behalf of the respondent that the signature in the written statement was not his signature. So the defendant's case ought not to have been considered and the plaintiffs suit ought to have been decreed ex parte. In the Present case defendant Nos. 2, 9 and 10 filed a joint written statement. but a separate written statement was filed by defendant No. 1 who has seriously contested the suit. He has not disowned his version appearing in the said written statement, rather he has led evidence to substantiate the same. In the present context, his utterance about his signature in the written statement appears to be a wrong recording. Apart from that had there been no written statement filed by the defendant, yet law requires that the plaintiff must prove his own case to the hilt by cogent and sufficient evidence. He cannot succeed merely on the weakness of the defence. Disbelief of the defence case ipso facto docs not make the plaintiffs case believable and if an authority is needed in this regard, we may profitably refer to a decision reported in 10 DLR (PC) page 1. Apart from that even in the case of an ex parte disposal of a suit, some requirements of law must be fulfilled before passing an ex parte decree in favour of the plaintiff by the Court. The Court is required to come to a finding on assessment of the materials on record that the plaintiff has been able to prove his case. In support of this view, a decision in the case of Bangladesh Vs. Abdul Wadud and others reported in 25 DLR (SC) page 90 may be referred to. Thus in any view of the matter the plaintiff must prove his case with sufficient evidence to obtain even an ex parte decree in his favour. In the present case, as we have already observed on consideration of the materials on record that the plaintiff has failed to prove his case with reliable and sufficient evidence and the bainanama Ext. 4 has been found to be a forged and fabricated one and not genuine, the claim of the plaintiff is therefore found to be false and the suit cannot be decreed in his favour. 

 30. Now let us consider the submissions of the learned Advocate for the appellants with regard to possession of the parties in the suit-land. It is true that no specific issue has been framed on possession, but both the sides adduced evidence in this regard and the Trial Court, of course, has held in deciding the question of limitation that the plaintiff is in possession of the suit land in part performance of the contract but he has not discussed the evidence of both the sides in juxtaposition. PW 3 is the plaintiff. He has stated that he has been living in the hut on the suit land. PW 4 is the alleged deed writer but he has not said anything about possession. PW 5 who is the mamashasur of the plaintiff has, of course, said something about the plaintiffs possession but none else from the side of the plaintiff has come to corroborate him. As against this evidence, the defendant has examined 4 DWs and all of them denied the possession of the plaintiff and asserted the possession of the defendants, particularly the subsequent transfer of defendant No. 1. Of course, it has been stated by some of the DWs that plaintiff was in possession of 2-3 kanis of the suit land for some time as bargadar under defendant No. 1. The plaintiff of course denied this assertion of the defendants. The fact remains that a money suit was instituted for barga crops against the present plaintiff and the same was decreed and against which a Misc. Case under Order 9 rule 13 was filed by the present plaintiff and the same was also dismissed for default and subsequently he instituted a regular suit against that ex parte decree which is still pending since 1974. In that suit of defendant No.1, the present plaintiff was found by the Court to be a bargachashi under the present defendant No. 1 and unless that finding is set aside by a competent Court, the validity of the said finding is still in force. So, the defendant's plea that the present plaintiff possessed some portion of the suit land for some time as bargachashi appears to be correct and in that view of the matter, the learned Subordinate Judge does not appear to have given a correct finding on the question of possession. Of course, with regard to the question of limitation, it has been rightly held that the suit is not barred by limitation. Article 113 provides for limitation in a suit for specific performance of contract and it is three years from the date fixed for performance of the same and if no such date is fixed when the plaintiff has noticed that performance is refused. In the instant case, the alleged agreement has been shown to have been made on 7.12.69 and it was according to the plaintiff stipulated therein that within three years from the date of execution of the bainapatra defendant No. 1 was required to execute the deed in his favour i.e. within 7.12.72. Of course, the plaintiff has stated that in May, 1971 he requested the defendant No.1 to execute the deed but the defendant No. 1 refused to do so, but this factum of request for the execution of the deed could not be established by the plaintiff on evidence and naturally 7.12.72 would be taken as the last date for executing the deed according to the terms of the alleged contract and from that date if three years of limitation is counted, it will be approximately 7.12.75 but this suit was instituted on the 30th September, 1974. So, it appears that the suit was filed within time. Now, from the judgment it appears that the learned Subordinate Judge in considering the capacity of the plaintiff to pay the earnest money as alleged, has spent much time on the alleged minority of the plaintiff to enter into the agreement. Now, here this question of minority has been raised in the context of financial capability. From this, it appears that the learned Subordinate Judge also decided the suit within a wrong premise. Now, as to the last submission of the learned Advocate for the appellant that even in case of success of the plaintiff in proving his case, because of the involvement of the third parties i.e. the subsequent purchasers namely, defendant Nos. 2-11, the passing of the decree may however be refused on payment of reasonable solatium to the plaintiff by the defendant No. 1 as the relief for specific performance of a contract under section 22 of the Specific Relief Act is a discretionary one. It is true that the relief under the Specific Relief Act as submitted is a discretionary one and in the light of the decision reported in BLD 1983 (AD) 225, the decree may be refused, but as we have already held that the plaintiff has miserably failed to prove the alleged contract and the payment of any earnest money, we do not deem it necessary to consider the above submission and make any finding thereon. 

 31. For the reasons stated above, we are of the view that the plaintiff has failed to prove his case by cogent and reliable evidence and as such he is not entitled to any relief for specific performance of the alleged contract. The findings as stated above and the impugned judgment and decree of the learned Subordinate Judge are therefore liable to be set aside.
